title: Why do small businesses still not have bank loans? Is it the firm, the loan price, or the bank? Guest post by Emma Zhang
gist: Job-market paper by Emma Zhang (Chicago Booth): referring 702 Pakistani SMEs to bank loan officers shows little aversion to banks; 90% of drop-off comes from SMEs abandoning loans over price/collateral, not denials. Loan officers do not pass on the State Bank of Pakistan's 9% promotional scheme (informed firms were 33% less likely to get a 9% quote), and default-penalty-averse officers price out borrowers rather than screen them.

themes.theme: Where SME loan applications break down

insights.claim: Low SME loan application rates in LMICs may be misread as low demand; they can reflect firms never reaching the bank, failing to get acceptable terms, or loan officers turning them away, nuances invisible in bank administrative data.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Bank admin data understates latent SME credit demand.
insights.locator: Many would declare that promotional interest

insights.claim: In a study of 702 Pakistani SMEs, 80% requested a referral to a bank and 51% had a real interaction with a loan officer, indicating little aversion to banks.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Demand for formal credit exists; the bottleneck is inside the bank.
insights.locator: We find very little aversion to the bank

insights.claim: The main drop-off point is after meeting a loan officer but before screening, where officers visit the business and regenerate accounting statements from transaction data.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Verification costs in credit-information-poor markets are a structural lending barrier.
insights.locator: We find very little aversion to the bank

insights.claim: Among SME-loan officer pairs that met but did not produce applications, 63% cited interest rate or collateral and 27% said the SME lost interest, so 90% of drop-off was SMEs giving up rather than officer denials.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Banks effectively ration via price, not denial.
insights.quote: 90% of dropoff was driven by SMEs giving up on the bank loan, and not by loan officer denials
insights.locator: We find that of the SME-loan officer pairs

insights.claim: In the control group the average quoted SME interest rate was 11%, 51% were asked for land or property collateral, and only 25% received a 9% rate or lower.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Collateral demands remain heavy despite 'collateral-free' schemes.

themes.theme: Promotional lending schemes fail at the loan officer

insights.claim: Every commercial bank in Pakistan advertises below-market SME lending schemes and all new small business loans are partially guaranteed by the central bank, yet loan officers were not offering promotional loans.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Subsidy and guarantee programs channeled via banks may not reach SMEs.
insights.locator: We find that loan officers were not offering

insights.claim: SMEs informed about the 9% State Bank of Pakistan Asaan Finance Scheme were 8 percentage points (33%) less likely to receive a 9% quote and were asked for 2 percentage points (19%) more interest.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Information campaigns about subsidized credit can backfire.
insights.quote: were actually 8pp (33%) less likely to receive a 9% quote from a loan officer, and they were asked for 2pp (19%) more interest
insights.locator: We find that loan officers were not offering

insights.claim: Promotional lending schemes are internally a way for banks to incentivize loan officers to offer lower rates, but head-office incentives to lend may not translate into benefits for loan officers.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Principal-agent problems inside banks blunt policy transmission.
insights.locator: Many would declare that promotional interest

insights.claim: Firms randomly referred to more default-concerned loan officers were 19 percentage points (88%) more likely to be quoted a high-interest, land- or property-collateralized loan, the most expensive type, and these officers were not more likely to screen.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Compensation design shapes credit pricing more than borrower risk.
insights.quote: were 19pp (88%) more likely to be quoted a high interest, land or property-collateralized loan
insights.locator: Additional to the information treatment effect

insights.claim: Default penalties in loan officer compensation appear to reduce lending effort rather than increase borrower verification, with lending commissions and bonuses insufficient to offset them.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Bank incentive structures may be suppressing SME loan growth in EMs.
insights.locator: This increase in loan price by default concern

insights.claim: Rather than credit rationing by denial, default-averse officers raise prices, which may adversely select the pool of borrowers willing to proceed.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Hidden adverse selection could raise SME loan book default rates.
insights.locator: This increase in loan price by default concern

insights.claim: Letting loan prices rise unregulated is undesirable for financial stability because higher rates induce adverse selection, excessive risk-taking, strategic default and loss of trust; the State Bank of Pakistan caps SME rates only after applications are submitted.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Regulatory caps miss pre-application price quotes.

insights.claim: With the World Bank making private capital mobilization a central pillar of its jobs strategy, targeting banks with interventions may not translate into supporting SMEs.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Skepticism warranted on bank-intermediated SME finance programs.
insights.quote: Our study highlights why targeting banks with interventions might not necessarily translate into supporting SMEs.
insights.locator: These findings also matter beyond Pakistan.
